analysis.one_liner: Raises the asset size at which big financial firms must undergo stress tests from $10 billion to $50 billion.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on May 16, 2017 and never received a hearing, vote, or any floor action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the post-2008 financial rules, large financial companies must regularly run 'stress tests' — simulations showing whether they could survive a severe recession — and report the results. This bill would have raised the asset threshold for those tests from $10 billion to $50 billion, freeing a tier of mid-sized banks from the requirement, and changed the required schedule from every six months or every year to simply 'periodic.' It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and died there without ever being debated or voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank and bank-holding companies with between $10 billion and $50 billion in assets. They would no longer have to run and publish their own stress tests on a fixed semiannual or annual schedule, cutting compliance costs. Their backers argued the fixed schedule burdened healthy regional banks with one-size-fits-all rules.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the stress-test rules to apply only to financial companies with $50 billion or more in consolidated assets, up from $10 billion, lifting the requirement off banks in the $10–50 billion range.
Changes required stress-test frequency from semiannual (for large companies) and annual (for others) to 'periodic,' leaving the schedule less fixed.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the added risk: stress tests are the early-warning system that showed regulators which banks could not survive a downturn, and weakening them for a tier of mid-sized banks means less visibility into weaknesses before a failure that taxpayers or the financial system could end up absorbing — the dynamic that followed the 2008 crisis.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via weakened bank oversight

drawbacks.text: Stress tests exist to catch a failing bank before it fails; raising the threshold to $50 billion removes that check on dozens of mid-sized banks whose failure could still ripple through the financial system.

Replacing fixed semiannual and annual schedules with vague 'periodic' testing removes a clear legal standard, leaving test frequency to regulators' discretion and making it easier for oversight to slip.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compliance savings to banks in the $10–50 billion range are real but modest, and 'periodic' testing already lets regulators tailor frequency. The cost is a weaker early-warning system for a class of banks big enough to cause real damage. The bill is a straightforward regulatory rollback for a segment of the industry, with the added risk borne diffusely by the public — which is why honest supporters framed it as tailoring, not repeal, and why the upside for ordinary people is essentially nil.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, vote, or moved it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Jon Tester introduced the bill on May 16, 2017, with Jerry Moran and Heidi Heitkamp as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019, having never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, mid-sized banks kept the stress-testing requirements they would have shed, and the post-crisis oversight framework remained unchanged during this Congress. The public came out ahead in the narrow sense that a rollback it would have paid for never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, since stress-test rules stayed

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 2 Democrats (Tester, Heitkamp) and 1 Republican (Moran) plus one more Republican cosponsor — but the bill never reached a vote, so no positional record exists beyond sponsorship.

industries.note: The bill's entire purpose was to lift annual and semiannual stress-testing requirements off this tier of banks, cutting their compliance costs. The savings are industry-side; the reduced early warning of bank weakness is a cost the public absorbs.

These banks were already below the $10 billion stress-test threshold, so the bill would not have changed their obligations directly. They are the constituency the 'Main Street' branding speaks to, though the relief in the bill goes to banks well above their size.
Banks above the new $50 billion threshold would remain subject to stress tests, though only 'periodically' rather than on a fixed semiannual or annual schedule — a modest loosening for them as well.
